name: Qualifying AI as a Drug Development Tool
blurb: The FDA ISTAND pilot and AI based clinical outcome tools.
title: Qualifying AI as a Drug Development Tool
answer: Some AI tools can be qualified once for a defined use and then relied on across many programmes. The FDA's ISTAND pilot, launched in November 2020, covers novel tools that do not fit the traditional qualification programmes, and it accepted its first AI based tool, an AI generated clinical outcome assessment.

reading.body:
Qualification lets one AI tool be accepted once for a defined use and then relied on across many programmes, instead of being defended in every submission.

The FDA created the ISTAND pilot in November 2020 for novel drug development tools that do not fit its existing qualification programmes for biomarkers, clinical outcome assessments and animal models. In 2024 it accepted the first AI based tool under that route, an AI generated clinical outcome assessment. Qualification is optional. A tool that is not qualified is simply assessed within each submission, and for a model used in a single programme that is usually the faster path.

The pattern is that regulatory acceptance of an AI tool can be a reusable asset rather than a per trial cost. That matters where the same model will support many trials, such as a digital measure of disease severity or an AI rated outcome. The value comes from repetition, so the case for qualifying a tool scales with how broadly it will be used.

The data covers two events and the eligibility rule, and no more. It does not say how long qualification takes, what evidence ISTAND requires, how many submissions the pilot has received, or whether any qualified AI tool is in use. It also does not connect to compute, buildings or power, because nothing here concerns the infrastructure an AI tool runs on.

Qualification shifts the unit of regulatory review from the trial to the tool. A sponsor that qualifies a model pays the evidence cost once and then cites that acceptance in every later submission, so the cost per programme falls as the number of programmes rises. A sponsor that does not qualify pays a smaller cost each time, but pays it repeatedly. The crossover point between the two paths depends on how many trials the tool will touch, which is why the route suits tools built for broad use and not tools built for one protocol.

The ISTAND route exists because the older qualification programmes are organized by category. Biomarkers, clinical outcome assessments and animal models each have their own track, and a novel tool that fits none of them had nowhere to go before November 2020. ISTAND is the catch-all for exactly that gap. The first AI based tool accepted under it, in 2024, was an AI generated clinical outcome assessment, which is notable because clinical outcome assessments already had a qualification track of their own. The pilot is not only absorbing tools with no home, it is also taking tools whose category exists but whose method is new.

The practical consequence for a life sciences team is a sequencing decision. Qualification is optional, and a tool assessed inside a single submission is assessed on that submission's terms. A team that expects one trial should defend the model in the submission. A team that expects a platform of trials should weigh the qualification evidence package against the sum of the per-submission defenses it would otherwise repeat. The data does not give the size of either cost, so the comparison has to be made with numbers from outside this page.

Who can apply to ISTAND?
Developers of novel drug development tools, which can include companies, consortia and academic groups.

Is qualification required to use an AI tool in a trial?
No. Qualification is optional, and without it the tool is assessed within each submission.

How long does ISTAND qualification take?
The data does not say. It records the November 2020 launch and the 2024 acceptance of the first AI based tool, but gives no timeline for a qualification from application to decision.

What evidence does ISTAND require from an AI tool?
The data does not hold this. It states only that qualification takes time and evidence, without describing what that evidence is.

How many submissions has the ISTAND pilot received?
The data does not say. It records only that the first AI based submission was accepted in 2024.

Is any qualified AI drug development tool in use today?
The data does not say. It covers the acceptance of a submission, not the qualification of a tool or its use in any programme.

What is the difference between ISTAND and the existing qualification programmes?
The existing programmes cover biomarkers, clinical outcome assessments and animal models. ISTAND was created for novel tools that do not fit those categories.

explainer:
Qualification is a way to get regulatory acceptance of a tool for a defined context of use once, so that sponsors can rely on it across many programmes without defending it each time. The FDA runs qualification programmes for biomarkers, clinical outcome assessments and animal models, and created ISTAND in 2020 for innovative tools that do not fit those categories.

AI tools are natural candidates when the same model will support many trials, for example a digital measure of disease severity or an AI rated outcome assessment. ISTAND accepted its first AI based submission, an AI generated clinical outcome assessment, which shows the route is open. Qualification takes time and evidence, so it suits tools intended for broad use. For a model used in one programme, defending it within that submission under the credibility framework is usually faster.

What qualification means

A drug development tool is a method, material or measurement used in developing medicines: a biomarker, a clinical outcome assessment, a disease model, or software. Regulators run programmes that qualify such tools for a defined context of use, so that once qualified, any sponsor can rely on the tool in that context without proving it again in each application. For AI, qualification offers a route to use a model, such as one that predicts disease progression or selects patients, across many programmes with regulatory confidence established once.

How the process works

A developer submits a letter of intent describing the tool and its intended context of use. If accepted, it prepares a qualification plan setting out the evidence it will gather, agrees it with the agency, and then submits the full package. The agency reviews and, if satisfied, publishes the qualification with the context of use that sponsors may rely on. The process takes years and the evidence standards are high, which is why few AI tools have completed it so far, but the FDA and EMA have both opened the door and discussed AI specific considerations.

Why it matters strategically

A qualified AI tool is a valuable asset: it can be licensed, it shortens regulatory discussions for every programme that uses it, and it signals that the agency accepts the method. Companies and consortia pursuing qualification are usually those with a tool that many sponsors could use, such as a digital endpoint derived from wearable data or a model that enriches trials for patients likely to progress. For a tool used by one sponsor in one programme, the ordinary route of justifying it within the application is faster.
